questions.q: How does Mara confirm why the audit's method couldn't have caught the 5 accounts, rather than just assuming it?
options: She interviews the auditor about their personal opinion
She reads the audit's own charter and checklist and confirms it contains no step instructing a check of direct Entra ID role or AWS IAM policy assignments
She re-runs the audit herself using the automation's data
She asks Howard Okonjo to make a ruling
questions.explain: Mara checks the audit's own documented scope and finds that querying direct, individual assignments was never written into the method at all -- confirming the gap directly rather than inferring it.

questions.q: What is the key distinction this lesson draws between a "methodology gap" and a "data error"?
options: There is no real difference between the two
A data error is a mistake within an otherwise-correct method; a methodology gap means the method itself, followed perfectly, is structurally incapable of seeing a category of access
A methodology gap only applies to Python scripts, never to human-run audits
A data error is always worse than a methodology gap
questions.explain: The audit team followed their checklist correctly -- the checklist itself simply never included a step for direct, individual assignments, which is a methodology gap rather than a mistake made while executing the method.

questions.q: Why does this lesson reject treating the finding as "the audit team's mistake"?
options: Because the audit team followed its documented checklist exactly as written -- the checklist never included a step for direct assignments, so nothing was omitted by error
Because Howard Okonjo forbids blaming anyone in any report
Because the audit team doesn't report to Howard Okonjo
Because mistakes never happen at Hartwell
questions.explain: The audit team executed their process correctly; the gap is in what the process was scoped to check, not in how it was carried out.

questions.q: Why does this lesson also reject framing this as simply "the automation being better"?
options: Because the automation actually performed worse in this case

Because the automation's broader check was a deliberate design decision made back in Lessons 8 and 9, and the audit's narrower scope was a separate, also-reasonable process decision -- neither tool is flawed, there's a gap between what one process checks and what the segment's sensitivity requires
Because the automation and the audit check exactly the same things
Because Mara built the automation to deliberately make the audit look bad
questions.explain: Both tools did exactly what they were built to do; the issue is a gap between the audit process's defined scope and the completeness the OT/SCADA segment's sensitivity actually requires, not a quality difference between the tools.

questions.q: What is the one clean conclusion Lessons 11 through 15 establish together?
options: The automation has a bug that overcounts accounts

The compliance audit's group-membership-only method is structurally unable to detect direct, individually-assigned access, which is exactly how 5 stale break-glass grants went undercounted for fourteen months
Hartwell should discontinue compliance audits entirely
The Substation 12 outage was caused by a cybersecurity breach
questions.explain: This is the precise, defensible conclusion the investigation has built toward: a scope gap in the audit's methodology, not a tooling bug, data error, or anyone's negligence.
